lesson.title: It's Not There, It's Locked, or It's Not What You Expect: File Exceptions
lesson.summary: Opening a file assumes the file exists, is readable, and is actually a file, and Python raises a specific runtime error for each of those assumptions when it turns out to be wrong.
lesson.body:
Every file-reading example you have seen so far quietly assumed the file was exactly where it was supposed to be. In practice that assumption fails constantly: a filename gets misspelled, a file gets moved or deleted, a program does not have permission to read a folder it does not own. Each of these is a runtime error, exactly the second category from the last chapter, valid Python code that fails because of a real condition encountered while running, not because of anything wrong with the code's grammar.

The most common file exception by far is FileNotFoundError, raised when you try to open a path that does not exist.

```python
with open("does_not_exist.csv", "r") as f:
    data = f.read()
```

Running this prints a traceback whose final line is:

```
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'does_not_exist.csv'
```

A few other file-related exceptions show up regularly enough to know by name. PermissionError happens when the operating system itself denies the access you asked for, for example trying to open a file for writing when you only have read permission on it. IsADirectoryError happens when the path you hand to open() turns out to actually be a directory rather than a file, so there is nothing for open() to read or write. UnicodeDecodeError connects directly back to the text-versus-binary chapter: it happens when you open a file in text mode with a particular encoding, but the bytes actually stored in the file do not form valid characters under that encoding, for instance opening a file that was really saved with a different encoding than the one you specified.

You will study the full mechanics of try and except blocks in a dedicated lesson, but it is worth seeing a preview here, because handling a missing file gracefully is one of the most common reasons to use one at all. Instead of letting the exception crash the program, you can catch it by name and decide what to do instead.

```python
try:
    with open("does_not_exist.csv", "r") as f:
        data = f.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("That file doesn't exist yet.")
```

This prints:

```
That file doesn't exist yet.
```

Instead of a traceback ending the program, the except clause named the exact exception type raised by the open() call, FileNotFoundError, and ran a friendlier response in its place. The program continues on afterward exactly as if nothing had gone wrong. The full details of how try and except work, including handling several exception types at once, belong to their own lesson, but keep this pattern in mind: whenever you write code that opens a file, you are trusting that the file will actually be there, and that trust is exactly what these exceptions exist to protect against.
